utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, again. Okay, if you could tell us the situation, whether you feel it would be okay to continue with the evidence or not, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I don't feel well. Yesterday, finally, this ventilator, which is right above my head, was closed. It constantly caused problems for me throughout the summer because I have to sit here for an hour and a half at a time, I can't move from this spot, and my shoulder area and back were very painful. And later this affected my organs as well, and it affected my concentration. So I am sluggish, mentally, and this is not my natural condition. Also, I believe that my nutrition -- my diet has been upset. I was in excellent condition when I arrived, but now everything is getting worse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that cross-examination of this witness is impracticable, according to your observation. But how about going on with hearing the examination-in-chief now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I could do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear your position, Mr. Tieger or Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There really is no examination-in-chief. It's simply a question of reading a summary of the witness's evidence and asking him to confirm that his amalgamated statement is his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But at least we can save some five or ten minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- if we do that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And for scheduling purposes: On Monday, we are supposed to sit in the morning, due to a recent change about court scheduling, so my intention is to sit until 2.30, in an extended format, to accommodate as much as possible the evidence of Mr. Fraser. So my understanding - I had to confirm this first - on Monday and Tuesday, we'll hear Mr. Fraser's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And with the indulgence of the staff and interpreters, and if it is agreeable to the parties, we'll sit from 9.00 to 2.30. And Tuesday, it hasn't been finalised whether we will sit in the morning or in the afternoon. That should be finalised by the end of today, and parties will be informed in due course. And the cross-examination of this witness will be conducted after Mr. Fraser's evidence is concluded. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. If that's what the Court wishes to do, that, I believe, is acceptable to Mr. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And he is around now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: He is, to the best of my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So can you bring him now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We need to draw the curtain?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, he is protected with image distortion, so not voice distortion, and he's not using a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Before Mr. Gaynor starts examining you, I'd like to show you the image that we'll broadcast. Pursuant to your request, we'll not broadcast your image. Those in the public gallery and outside cannot see you. If the Audio Unit could kindly show his image. This is what will be seen outside. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, could you state your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Bogdan Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you, on the 28th of September, 2010, read a statement which contained relevant parts of the transcripts of your evidence in the trials of Stanislav Galic and Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were you given an opportunity to make any corrections that you wished to make to that statement?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You didn't wish to make any corrections?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, no corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I ask the Registrar, please, for 65 ter 90194, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, on the screen in front of you, do you see the first page of your amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Would you provide the same answers if you were asked, under oath, about those topics today?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And with the Court's permission, I will now read a summary of Mr. Vidovic's evidence for the benefit of the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Or go ahead, Ram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. You have an objection to the admission of that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, a couple of parts of it. There are two incidents that are included in that statement that are unscheduled incidents. On page 41 is an unscheduled incident on the 14th of February, 1995, the sniping of a tram. And on pages 41 through 48, there is the shelling of Omladinska Street on the 11th of July, 1994. And pursuant to the arguments that we've made earlier that you've rejected, we, nevertheless, wish to preserve that objection by asking that those incidents be redacted from the amalgamated statement, that no associated exhibits be admitted concerning those incidents, and that evidence concerning these unscheduled incidents not be received. And I realise that you have already ruled that these are relevant for pattern and widespread and systematic elements of the offences that Dr. Karadzic is charged with, but I would just like to point out that, in order for them to be useful in that way, you would have to conclude that it was the Bosnian Serbs that were responsible for those shellings, because if it wasn't, then it's not part of any pattern that's of any relevance to the charges and, therefore, it's necessary for us to bring evidence to rebut that assertion. So these decisions to admit unscheduled incidents have an affect upon the resources and the time that will be spent during the course of this trial. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you wish to hear from me on this point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not now, Mr. Gaynor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We ruled upon this matter, as you indicated, and you kindly referred to the reasoning, so I don't feel the need to repeat it. Your objection is overruled. Yes, Judge Morrison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, I appreciate the reason why you're doing it. I see that it's not frivolous. You're following the American pattern concerning things which might be considered for appellate purposes later, no doubt. As I understand it, in American law, if you don't raise it ab initio, you can't raise it on appeal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct. It's also my understanding of the law of this Tribunal the Appeals Chamber sometimes dismisses grounds of appeal that haven't been raised by the Trial Chamber, so that's why we feel the need to raise it on a continuing basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That's what I thought. As you will understand, in the UK, that's not the position, so sometimes UK judges find continual raising of these matters frivolous, but be assured I don't, because I understand the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have to wait for translation. Only now the translation has been complete. Yes, we'll give the number to that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P1742.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I also seek at this stage the admission of the associated exhibits, which are referred to on pages 63 and 64 of the amalgamated statement? The very last entry on page 64 is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll raise it after you read out the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll now read the summary of the evidence, Mr. President. Mr. Vidovic joined the Criminal Department of the Security Services Centre (CSB) of the RBiH MUP in Sarajevo in November 1992. He describes the training he received and the duties he performed as a criminal forensic technician for CSB Sarajevo, during which he was involved in the investigation of a considerable number of shelling and sniping incidents. In his previous evidence, Mr. Vidovic authenticated documentation relating to an incident in which a tram, travelling west on Smaja od Bosne Street towards Alipasino Polje, was hit by sniper fire on the 19th of June, 1994. The investigative team concluded that the bullet had fragmented upon impact with a heating and ventilation unit in the middle of the tram, resulting in injury to three passengers. The investigative team concluded that the bullet had come from the direction of Grbavica and Vrace, which were under Bosnian Serb control. Mr. Vidovic was also involved in the investigation of a shelling incident that occurred on the 16th of June, 1995. In this incident, a modified air-bomb exploded at number 7 on Cobanija Street, inflicting physical injuries to three people and extensive property damage. Mr. Vidovic also discussed a sniping incident on the 14th of February, 1995, in which a tram, going from Bascarsija towards the depot at Alipasino Polje, was shot at. One passenger was injured. The shot was determined to have come from the south-east. Mr. Vidovic was also involved in the investigation of a shelling incident at Omladinska Street on 11th of July, 1995, and authenticated documentation relating to this incident. Mr. Vidovic described an incident in which he and members of his investigative team came under sniper fire while conducting an investigation into a shelling incident near the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo. He states that, as a general matter, anti-sniping barricades, in the form of large metal containers which were set up at intersections, provided cover to people from gun-fire coming from Serb-held positions. However, the containers only offered limited protection. Sometimes a bullet would pass through a container and hit a person behind it, and sometimes snipers would fire over a container onto people behind it. Mr. Vidovic's father was killed by shelling on 6th of October, 1992, when he was coming back from getting water from a water tank which was located close to the family's apartment building in the center of Sarajevo. Mr. Vidovic states that approximately 50 shells fell in the area around his family's apartment building between 1992 and 1995. That concludes the summary. I'd now like to seek the admission of the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How many of them, in total; 22?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them have actually -- have been admitted already. I think Mr. Doraiswamy has the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you indicate what documents have been already admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then I'll raise them one by one. First, could you take a look at the sixth item, the 65 ter number of which is 10509 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- which are medical records relating to persons admitted to the University Medical Centre. But reading the statements, but the witness didn't mention anything but that it was some kind of medical finding. So on that basis, whether it can be admitted as an associated exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if you're minded, you can go -- and number 14, 65 ter 09659 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- letter from Karavelic, and also the witness did not speak to the contents about this. All the witness did was to read or confirm what had been written on the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And number 15, the next one, letter from President Izetbegovic, also the same is true with that item as well. And I'm not quite sure about the last item, which is not numbered, which refers to a report concerning the shelling of Cobanija Street, which is allegedly attached to the ICTY witness statement. Are you tendering this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. I'll clarify those points in turn. First of all, as Your Honour pointed out, a number of the documents which were put to the witness during his cross-examination in his previous evidence were put to him by the Defence teams in those cases, and he was not able to add a great deal of value to those documents. And these were documents emanating from the ABiH or from, in one case, President Izetbegovic. Now, we took the position that we would err on the side of inclusiveness, so we have included those in the package of associated exhibits. We certainly have no objection if Your Honours wish to remove those. We certainly don't object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're referring to number 14 and 15?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. President. The other point you raised was the very final document or report concerning the Cobanija Street. This was, in fact -- this is, in fact, the first document on the previous page. It was inserted in there, I think, simply to note that it was originally attached to the witness's statement -- to the witness statement of KDZ438 on the 10th of March, 1997. So Your Honours can essentially ignore that particular entry, as it refers to a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. How about the medical records?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. If -- again, I understand the point that the witness was not able to confirm the medical basis for these. And if Your Honours do not wish to admit them as an integral part of his evidence, perhaps they could be admitted as an associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. In order to be admitted as an associated exhibit, it should form an indispensable and inseparable part of the statement. But it is not the case. So if you want to tender that, you have to go through it with the witness. But in relation to the two letters emanating from the cross-examination, if there's no objection, the Chamber is minded to admit them, both of them. So you would like to tender that medical record, number 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. If there's no objection from the other side, we'd like to tender it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then on that basis, we'll admit them all. And the numbers of those exhibits will be circulated in due course by the Court Officer. Mr. Vidovic, I have to apologise to you. Due to the condition of the accused, who is not feeling well at this moment, we cannot continue with his cross-examination. And, moreover, we have set Monday and Tuesday for a specific witness who had difficulty travelling to The Hague, so we will resume your evidence, i.e., cross-examination by the accused, on Wednesday. And the proper time has not been finalised, but it will be informed to you by the Victim and Witness Section. Unless there's anything else to be raised --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- the hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 18th day of October, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.06 p.m.,
